conventions.convention: Curve derivatives are domain-relative, including one-sided derivatives at included interval endpoints; the curve-calculus statements require at least two interval points.
Masses are positive constants; labels range from 1 through N. In the two-body split, r=x₁−x₂ and μ=m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂).
Pair force fᵢⱼ contributes to label i, satisfies fᵢⱼ=−fⱼᵢ, and contributes internal torque (xᵢ−xⱼ)×fᵢⱼ for i<j. Centrality means fᵢⱼ=λᵢⱼ(xᵢ−xⱼ), including the coincident-position case.
The potential on I×Q is restricted from a C¹ function on J×Q, with J open and containing I; its partial derivatives are restricted derivatives of that extension.

Continuation requires a compact subset of the open time-state domain containing the terminal graph. State trapping alone is the autonomous alternative on D=ℝ×U. The escape corollary asserts an outside point in every terminal neighborhood, rather than stating eventual permanent departure.

Distribution pairings are complex-linear in the test, with no conjugation; u′(φ)=−u(φ′), [p]=p(t*+)−p(t*−), and the representative value at the jump does not affect the distribution. Countable Choice is assumed.
J is the impulse on label 1 and −J on label 2. Restitution is the full-vector equation v₂⁺−v₁⁺=−e(v₂⁻−v₁⁻), with 0≤e≤1; ΔK is post-impact minus pre-impact kinetic energy.

The variable-mass theorem adopts both m′=r_in−r_out and (mv)′=F+r_in w_in−r_out w_out; exchanged velocities are the supplied velocities, and the relative-velocity acceleration equation is a product-rule deduction.

load_bearing.statement: For x,y:I→ℝ³ and λ:I→ℝ differentiable at t₀ on an interval with at least two points, sums, λx, inner products, cross products and squared norms are differentiable there, with their stated sum and product rules; (‖x‖₂²)′=2⟨x′,x⟩.

For continuous F:D→ℝⁿ on open D⊆ℝ×ℝⁿ, locally Lipschitz in the state variable locally uniformly in time, a solution x:[t₀,b)→ℝⁿ whose terminal graph lies in a compact K⊆D extends to [t₀,b+ε) for some ε>0. For autonomous F on ℝ×U, terminal trapping in compact K₀⊆U also suffices.

For N≥1, positive constant masses and differentiable curves on an interval with at least two points, X=M⁻¹Σmᵢxᵢ and ρᵢ=xᵢ−X satisfy Σmᵢρᵢ=Σmᵢρᵢ′=0 and Σmᵢ‖xᵢ′‖₂²=M‖X′‖₂²+Σmᵢ‖ρᵢ′‖₂²; for N=2 the relative term is μ‖(x₁−x₂)′‖₂².
Assuming Countable Choice, for p on an open interval that is C¹ off t* and has finite one-sided limits of p and p′, p and its regular derivative are locally integrable and (u_p)′=u_(p′_reg)+[p]δ_t*.
For positive masses, twice differentiable x:I→Q, a potential with the stated C¹ extension, and mᵢxᵢ″=−∇ᵢU(t,x)+dᵢ, (K+U(t,x))′=∂ₜU(t,x)+Σ⟨dᵢ,xᵢ′⟩. If dᵢ≡0 and ∂ₜU≡0, this energy is constant on I.

For twice differentiable finite curve families with positive constant masses and pᵢ′=fᵢ+Σⱼ≠ᵢfᵢⱼ, fᵢⱼ=−fⱼᵢ, P′=Σfᵢ and J′=Σxᵢ×fᵢ+Σᵢ<ⱼ(xᵢ−xⱼ)×fᵢⱼ. The internal torque vanishes under the stated pairwise centrality hypothesis.
For differentiable m:I→(0,∞) and v:I→ℝ³, nonnegative exchange rates and the two stated material balance identities, mv′=F+r_in(w_in−v)−r_out(w_out−v).

Assuming Countable Choice and the stated continuous-force, piecewise-C² curve and impulse-pairing hypotheses, the momentum jumps are J and −J. With full-vector restitution e∈[0,1], the post-impact velocities are uniquely determined and ΔK=−(1−e²)μ‖v₂⁻−v₁⁻‖₂²/2.

alerts.finding: Clause (i) requires 'a motion ... of the associated first-order system ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]])'. That definition's clause (c) requires a C² motion satisfying the smooth equation throughout its interval, so its velocity cannot jump at an interior t*. This conflicts with the intended nonzero-impulse extension. The same postulate says 'its distributional rendering by test-function pairings is proved in [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]]'; that supplier instead assumes the pairings and continuous time-only regular forces, then derives the jumps. It does not prove the asserted converse for the postulate's evaluated state-dependent forces, whose one-sided values can differ.

The first Remarks bullet says 'equivalently the force map of an impulse model is not continuous across t*'. This does not follow from smooth-motion exclusion. The batch-2 impulse theorem explicitly permits continuous regular forces F₁,F₂, including zero forces, together with a nonzero additional Dirac impulse and discontinuous velocity. Continuity of the regular force map and existence of an impulse are compatible; it is the full smooth-motion equation across the event that fails. Also, L1 invokes the distributional supplier without establishing its pairing hypotheses from the finite-jump postulate; the finite velocity and energy algebra is independently immediate, but the models should not be identified.

L2 states 'K=M‖V‖₂²/2+μ‖d⁻‖₂²/2 before and after'. The post-impact split requires d⁺, not d⁻. For this example V=0, μ=3/2 and ‖d⁻‖=4, so the quoted formula gives K=12 J after every impact, whereas the sticking case has K⁺=0. The companion page cm15-scattering-and-impulse-model-boundaries-examples also says 'the elastic case exchanges the velocities'; the item's incoming velocities are 3n and −n, while its elastic outgoing velocities are −3n and n, so they are not exchanged.

Clause (c) writes 'the state curve z=(x,x′):J→D' and 'z(t)∈D', while clause (a) defines D=I₀×Q×ℝ^(3N), a time-state domain. The pair z=(x,x′) belongs to U=Q×ℝ^(3N); (t,z(t)) belongs to D. This is a local typing error; the associated equations and continuation consumer distinguish these objects correctly elsewhere.

seams_checked.note: Continuation L3–L4 preserves open-domain compact trapping and the extended-time autonomous qualification. The consumer's escape conclusion retains the supplier's terminal-neighborhood quantifiers.
Finite positive masses, pair antisymmetry, curve regularity and potential regularity are retained. Moving-origin and integrated-work additions use separate local arguments.
Pairing and curve-calculus citations are used for the stated differentiable curves; central-force assumptions and reduced-mass interpretation are supplied separately.
The external-force counterexample uses the sum and difference derivative rules without claiming centrality alone supplies relative reduction.
Rheonomic power applies work-energy to residual plus reaction forces. Its C² potential on open I₀×Q supplies the required C¹ extension for the motion interval.
The principal-axis stationary-point remark uses the inner-product derivative on differentiable unit-vector curves; continuous-material splitting comes from its separate measure-theoretic supplier.
Euler power uses the pairing rule; torque-free continuation uses a locally Lipschitz autonomous field on ℝ³ and compact state trapping.

Scattering continuation and variable-mass uses are faithful. The impulse postulate reverses the distributional supplier's deduction direction and the impact theorem conflates regular-force continuity with absence of an additional impulse; see alerts.

Rocket and control-volume product-rule uses preserve the balances. Impact-check L2 falsely retains d⁻ in the post-impact kinetic split. The e=2 counterexample correctly derives its hypothetical extension locally rather than applying the e∈[0,1] theorem.
The recurrence example uses compact energy-state trapping for a smooth autonomous mechanical field; backward continuation is the time-reflected application.
Smooth-dependence and stability consumers retain compact trapping inside the open ODE domain, with C¹ fields supplying local Lipschitz continuity.
Pairing derivatives and compact continuation are used with collision-excluded open domains. Uniqueness is separately attributed to Picard–Lindelöf, rather than to continuation alone.
Linearization and averaging continuation uses require compact terminal trapping; the nonautonomous averaging field has open domain ℝ×O and locally uniform state-Lipschitz bounds.
The adiabatic-drift example states autonomous compact-state continuation with the ODE regularity hypotheses.
Principal-axis stability and instability use the polynomial Euler field on ℝ³ with explicit local Lipschitz bounds and compact state traps.
The rescaled pulse-map argument cites compact continuation for its smooth field and compact time-state tube; it does not infer continuation from pointwise finiteness.
The lift proof uses compact products of interior closed time intervals with S³. It explicitly reflects time for the left endpoint and does not extend beyond the prescribed open time window.
